NSA arbitration entities asked to provide information to Congress

House Energy & Commerce Ranking Member Frank Pallone (D-N.J.) requested information from six certified independent dispute resolution entities seeking details on how each company conducts arbitration and compliance with the No Surprises Act (NSA). He expressed concern that the Independent Dispute Resolution (IDR) process is not functioning as intended and is resulting in increased out-of-pocket expenses and premiums for patients. The number of NSA-related provider-insurer disputes going to arbitration has far exceeded initial predictions, and these entities earn revenue for each dispute they resolve. The companies were given until Sept. 24 to respond.

OMS named as NIDCR director

National Institutes of Health (NIH) Director Jay Bhattacharya, MD, PhD, announced the selection of AAOMS Fellow Jonathan E. Burke, DMD, as Director of the National Institute of Dental and Craniofacial Research (NIDCR).

As noted in the press release, Dr. Burke served as the Medical Director of an oral and maxillofacial consulting firm in Philadelphia at the time of his appointment. He previously served as Assistant Professor of Surgery at the Robert Wood Johnson Medical School in New Brunswick, N.J., and concurrently held a Clinical Assistant Professor appointment at the Temple University School of Dentistry. Earlier in his career, Dr. Burke served as principal or co-investigator on research spanning TMJ pharmacology, implant devices and post-surgical pain management and has co-authored peer-reviewed articles and book chapters on craniofacial trauma, reconstruction and TMJ disorders. He received his doctorate in dental medicine from Temple University and completed his residency there as well.

NIDCR is one of the 27 institutes and centers of NIH and is focused on leading scientific research on dental, oral and craniofacial health and disease. Dr. Burke attended the AAOMS Annual Meeting in Seattle and spoke with members of the OMS research community about key areas of focus for the agency.

Report legislative connections to AAOMS

Advocacy relies on relationships. Oral and maxillofacial surgeons play a crucial role in shaping the future of their specialty. By becoming a key contact for members of Congress, members can directly influence healthcare policy, protect the profession and ensure patients continue to receive the care they need. Reporting these connections and communications back to AAOMS strengthens the specialty’s collective advocacy.

Join the Capitol Contact Campaign to help build stronger ties on Capitol Hill and advance the issues that matter most. To get involved, reach out to advocacy@aaoms.org.

Save the Date: 26th annual Day on the Hill

Make the specialty’s collective voice heard in Washington, D.C.! Join colleagues from across the country March 16 and 17 for the 26th annual AAOMS Day on the Hill. Connect with members of Congress and their staff, advocate for the specialty, gain firsthand insight into the legislative process and network with fellow AAOMS members and leaders. A new Congress means new opportunities to build relationships and educate lawmakers about oral and maxillofacial surgery.

Registration opens Nov. 9. A limited number of funding spots will be available for complimentary round-trip airfare and one night of hotel accommodations. Funding will be offered first-come, first-served to fellows and members who have not attended an in-person Day on the Hill within the past five years.

Visit AAOMS.org/DayontheHill for registration and full event details.

Federal Affairs

Congress considers healthcare measures before elections

Before the House adjourned for the midterm elections, the House Energy and Commerce Committee held a hearing on various healthcare proposals, including several bills aimed at reforming Medicare physician payments.

The Patients First Act (HR 9693), which AAOMS largely supports, was among the bills that received the most attention. The bill would provide an annual inflationary update to physician reimbursement, increase the budget neutrality threshold and replace the current Merit-based Incentive Payment System (MIPS) with a new physician quality payment program.

The committee also considered the Dental and Optometric Care (DOC) Access Act (HR 1521), which is led by the ADA and supported by AAOMS. The bill would prohibit federally regulated dental plans from setting fees for services the plans do not cover.

The Health Care Cybersecurity and Resiliency Act of 2026 (S 3315) also was discussed during the hearing. Among other provisions, the bill would mandate minimum cybersecurity practices for HIPAA-regulated entities – including multifactor authentication, encryption of protected health information and alignment with national frameworks – while allowing HHS enforcement discretion for entities facing extraordinary compliance burdens. The Senate passed this bill on Sept. 30, just before adjourning for the midterm elections, increasing the bill’s chances of passing the House as part of a post-election lame-duck package.

DHS proposed visa rule exempts most physicians and dentists

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) recently released a proposed rule that would impose a $103,265 fee on employers sponsoring H-1B visa workers; however, the proposed rule excludes “cap-exempt H-1B petitions,” which are `typically used to sponsor internationally born physicians and dentists. Therefore, the new fee should not apply to most internationally born physicians and dentists who are in the U.S. or would traditionally come to the U.S. on an H-1B visa.

President Trump tried to impose a fee last year via proclamation that would apply to physicians and dentists. The fee was halted pending legal challenges. AAOMS, along with other organizations representing healthcare professionals, commented against the fee and also supported the Physicians and Healthcare Workforce Act (HR 7961), which would exempt physicians, dentists and other healthcare workers from the fee and prevent future H-1B fees beyond those currently authorized by federal law.

HRSA awards dental care access grants

HHS, through the Health Resources Services Administration (HRSA), announced that 28 HRSA-funded health centers would receive $51 million in awards to improve access to dental care for children with neurodevelopment disorders. The new Quality Improvement Fund – Improving Access to Dental Services for Children with Neurodevelopmental Disorders (QIF-DNDD) will help health centers build on evidence-based models and test innovative approaches to improve dental care for children with such disorders as autism spectrum disorder, Down syndrome, cerebral palsy and intellectual disabilities. The work will aid HRSA and health centers in identifying patient-focused, long-term approaches that can be replicated in other health centers and communities.

State Affairs

States shift to election mode

With most state legislatures having completed their regular sessions for the year, legislative activity has slowed as lawmakers turn their attention to the Nov. 3 elections.

Voters in 46 states will elect more than 6,100 state legislators this fall, representing more than 80 percent of state legislative seats nationwide. While most statehouses are now quiet, some lawmakers will return after Election Day for veto, lame duck or other post-election sessions. Illinois, for example, has a November–December veto session scheduled, while several other legislatures remain in session through year-end.

The transition to 2027 also will begin quickly. Maine’s newly elected legislature convenes in early December, with most other states returning after the new year.

AAOMS will continue monitoring state legislative and regulatory activity through the remainder of 2026 while preparing for issues affecting OMSs that may emerge in 2027.

D.C. grants CRNA opt-out status despite opposition

Washington, D.C., has opted out of the federal physician supervision requirement for CRNAs, joining 27 states that have taken similar action. The decision allows CRNAs practicing in District hospitals to provide anesthesia without the federal physician supervision requirement. D.C. previously authorized independent CRNA practice through its Health Occupations Revision General Amendment Act of 2024.

AAOMS joined the American Society of Anesthesiologists, American Medical Association, D.C. Society of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgeons and other medical organizations in an Aug. 17 letter urging Mayor Muriel Bowser to reject the opt-out. The organizations argued physician involvement remains an important patient-safety safeguard and said evidence has not demonstrated that opt-out policies improve anesthesia access, cost or quality.

Practice Management

Transparency in Coverage rule finalized

The Internal Revenue Service, Employee Benefits Security Administration and HHS released the final Transparency in Coverage Rule on Oct. 6. This rule sets forth requirements regarding price transparency reporting for non-grandfathered group health plans and health insurance issuers offering non-grandfathered group and individual health insurance. The agencies intend to improve the standardization, accuracy and accessibility of public pricing disclosures.

While the finalized rules do not alter the disclosure requirements for OMSs, health plans and health insurance issuers will be required to provide participants, beneficiaries or enrollees with specific information about coverage and pricing for both in-network and out-of-network services. More information will be made publicly available about contracted rates and coverage utilization, organized by provider network to allow for better comparison. Additionally, this rule creates new requirements regarding the disclosure of balance billing limitations and cost-sharing estimates and specifies the way this information must be available via phone and in online self-service portals.

OMSs should remain alert for communications from contracted health plans to ensure compliance with any new data disclosure requests. The provisions of this final rule are effective on Dec. 7.

UHC announces codes no longer requiring PA

UnitedHealthcare (UHC) issued a pledge in May 2026 to reduce prior authorizations (PA) by 30 percent before the end of 2026. The payer recently released a list of 1,700 specific procedure codes to be exempt from PA, effective Oct. 1.

Several OMS-rendered procedures are included on this list for commercial, Medicare Advantage, dual-special needs plans, individual exchanges and UHC Community Plans. Debridement codes, excision of benign lesions, wound repair, autografts, destruction of benign lesions, biopsies, removal of foreign body, trigger point injections, excision of benign tumors or cysts, intranasal biopsy and uvulectomy are now exempt from prior authorization.

Full lists of the exempted procedures can be found on the UHC website. OMSs are encouraged to remain up-to-date with payer policy revisions and trends.

Be aware of CMS EPCS Program requirements

OMSs should be aware of the CMS Electronic Prescribing for Controlled Substances (EPCS) Program. Under this program, at least 70 percent of Schedule II, III, IV and V controlled substances prescribed by a practitioner under Medicare Part D and Medicare Advantage prescription drug plans (MA-PD) must be electronic prescriptions. This mandate applies to any doctor prescribing under Medicare Part D or MA-PD Plans, even if opted out of Medicare. The CMS EPCS is separate from state e-prescribing programs, and there is no registration process – the program automatically calculates prescriber compliance using Medicare Part D plan data.

CMS automatically exempts prescribers who issue 100 or fewer qualifying Medicare Part D controlled substances and prescribers located in the geographic area of a declared federal, state or local emergency or disaster. Prescribers may also apply for a program waiver for circumstances that prevent them from meeting program requirements; these circumstances include technological limitations among others, reviewed on a case-by-case basis. The waiver application period is open from September to November each year; this year it closes on Nov. 18 at 8 p.m. EST.

More information about the CMS EPCS program, including waiver criteria and timelines, can be found on the CMS EPCS website. OMSs can also use this website to verify their waiver and compliance status.

OSHA releases workplace guidance for opioid emergencies

The U.S. Department of Labor’s Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) released a fact sheet to help employers and workers respond to opioid-related overdose emergencies in the workplace. OSHA’s new guidance, “Opioid Overdose Rescue with Reversal Medications,” highlights overdose preparedness strategies. Part of the Great American Recovery Initiative, a government-wide effort prioritizing addiction treatment and recovery, this guidance empowers workplaces to recognize the signs of an overdose and act immediately.
